source: Aruna Ranganathan and Xingqi Maggie Ye, 'AI Doesn't Reduce Work—It Intensifies It', Harvard Business Review (Digital Article), published February 9, 2026. Opened: https://hbr.org/2026/02/ai-doesnt-reduce-work-it-intensifies-it (full article body read from the page's embedded article data). Also opened: Laura Counts, 'Does AI Actually Free up Workers' Time?', UC Berkeley Research, February 18, 2026, https://vcresearch.berkeley.edu/node/29618 (Q&A with Ye).
data_type: Ethnography (in-person observation, internal communication channels, semi-structured interviews). Described by the authors as 'in-progress research'. No quantitative measures reported.
sample_and_method: One U.S.-based technology company 'with about 200 employees'. 'From April to December last year [2025], we studied how generative AI tools changed work habits at the tech company. We did this through in-person observation two days a week, tracking internal communication channels, and more than 40 in-depth interviews across engineering, product, design, research, and operations.' The Berkeley Q&A calls it an 'eight-month ethnography' with 'more than 40 semi-structured interviews across functional groups'; Ye attended meetings and everyday conversations. The company 'did not mandate AI use (though it did offer enterprise subscriptions to commercially available AI tools).' How the company or interviewees were recruited is not stated.
vendor_interest: No. Authors are UC Berkeley Haas academics; HBR is a management publisher that does not sell AI or measurement tooling. The studied company is unnamed.
headline_figures: No quantitative findings. The only figures are sample descriptors: 'In an eight-month study of how generative AI changed work habits at a U.S.-based technology company with about 200 employees, we found that employees worked at a faster pace, took on a broader scope of tasks, and extended work into more hours of the day, often without being asked to do so.' and 'more than 40 in-depth interviews across engineering, product, design, research, and operations.'
metric_layer: None measured numerically. Qualitative observation of work activity and workload (pace, scope, hours, multitasking). Touches quality only as a projected risk ('lower quality work'), not measured.
respondent_role_split: No numeric split. Qualitative role effects: 'Product managers and designers began writing code; researchers took on engineering tasks'; 'engineers, in turn, spent more time reviewing, correcting, and guiding AI-generated or AI-assisted work produced by colleagues', including coaching colleagues who were 'vibe-coding' and finishing partially complete pull requests. No manager/director/executive split.
workload_signal: Central to the piece. Three forms of intensification: task expansion (workers 'absorbed work that might previously have justified additional help or headcount'), blurred boundaries (prompting during lunch, meetings, a 'quick last prompt' before leaving; work spilling into evenings or early mornings; 'downtime no longer provided the same sense of recovery'), and more multitasking ('continual switching of attention, frequent checking of AI outputs, and a growing number of open tasks'). Engineers took on extra review and correction of colleagues' AI-assisted work, often informally in Slack or desk-side. Pressure came not from mandates but norms: 'this rhythm raised expectations for speed—not necessarily through explicit demands, but through what became visible and normalized'. 'Many workers noted that they were doing more at once—and feeling more pressure—than before they used AI'. Projected consequences: workload creep, cognitive fatigue, burnout, weakened decision-making, turnover.
definition_of_value_offered: Partly. The authors do not define a payoff metric, but warn that short-run output can mislead: 'What looks like higher productivity in the short run can mask silent workload creep and growing cognitive strain' and overwork can 'make it harder for organizations to distinguish genuine productivity gains from unsustainable intensity.' Their remedy is an 'AI practice': 'a set of intentional norms and routines that structure how AI is used, when it is appropriate to stop, and how work should and should not expand in response to newfound capability', built from intentional pauses (e.g. a decision pause requiring one counterargument and one link to organizational goals), sequencing (batching notifications, protecting focus windows) and human grounding. Implied definition: gains count only if sustainable and not bought with hidden extra load.
removal_counterfactual: None. No comparison group or period without AI tools; contrasts with pre-AI work are participants' retrospective accounts (e.g. tasks they 'would have outsourced, deferred, or avoided entirely in the past').
key_quotes: 1. 'You had thought that maybe, oh, because you could be more productive with AI, then you save some time, you can work less. But then really, you don't work less. You just work the same amount or even more.' (engineer quoted in HBR) 2. 'Our findings suggest that without intention, AI makes it easier to do more—but harder to stop.' (authors, HBR). Note: both quotes contain em dashes or will need paraphrase/ellipsis for site style; quote 2's em dash is in the original.
caveats: Single company of about 200 people, unnamed, U.S. tech sector; qualitative and in-progress, not peer reviewed at time of publication. No measures of hours, output or burnout; consequences such as burnout, turnover and lower quality are presented as risks ('can'), not observed outcomes. Causation inferred from interviews and observation. Some secondary coverage reports the sample as '40 workers' or 'about 200 employees' interchangeably; the primary says the company had about 200 employees and the authors did more than 40 interviews plus observation. The Berkeley Q&A dates Ye's affiliation as 'PhD 28'.
access: Primary opened in full: HBR article text was present in the page's embedded data (article is paywall-eligible; full body extracted and read). Berkeley summary opened in full. Not verified: any underlying working paper or interview data (none linked).
